---
title: "How a .qmd works"
subtitle: "The building blocks of every page on this site"
---

::: {.callout-note}
## Instructor cue
Keep the `.qmd` source open on the left and this rendered page on the right. Scroll both together. Students do not need R running to follow.
:::

A Quarto document (`.qmd`) mixes three things in one file:

1. **A YAML header**: configuration at the very top, between two lines of `---`.
2. **Markdown prose**: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images.
3. **Code chunks**: R code that runs when you render, with its output placed right where the chunk sits.

Rendering turns the source into an output: a web page, a PDF, a slide deck. Same source, different output, one click.

## 1. The YAML header

The header of this very page looks like this:

```yaml
---
title: "How a .qmd works"
subtitle: "The building blocks of every page on this site"
---
```

Everything else about how the page looks (theme, table of contents, folded code) comes from `_quarto.yml`, the project-wide configuration, so you set it once and every page inherits it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Live experiment
Change `title:` in the source, save, render. The page title updates. That is the entire feedback loop of Quarto: edit, render, look.
:::

## 2. Markdown prose

Plain text is a paragraph. A line starting with `##` is a section heading (and appears in the table of contents on the right). `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `` `code` ``, and lists:

- a bullet
- another bullet

work the way you expect. You are writing a document, not a program.

## 3. Code chunks

A chunk is fenced by three backticks with `{r}` on the opening fence:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
cafe <- read_csv("data/cafe_transactions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(cafe)
```

The code ran and its result is printed below it. Chunk options start with `#|` on the first lines of the chunk and control things like whether the code shows (`echo`), whether it runs (`eval`), and figure size:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(cafe, aes(x = unit_price)) + geom_histogram()
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Why chunks matter for your project
Your Milestone 1 numbers must be executed, not typed. A chunk that prints `nrow(cafe)` can never drift from the data. A number you typed into a sentence can.
:::

## 4. Inline R: numbers that never drift

You can put R inside a sentence. This sentence is computed: the dataset has `r nrow(cafe)` transactions across `r n_distinct(cafe$store)` stores, and `r sum(is.na(cafe$unit_price))` rows have a missing price.

The source of that sentence is:

```markdown
the dataset has `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(cafe)")` transactions
```

If the data changes, the sentence changes. That is what "reproducible" means in practice.

## 5. Callouts

The colored boxes on this page are callouts. They are one line of markup:

```markdown
::: {.callout-tip}
## A title
Some text.
:::
```

Five kinds exist: `note`, `tip`, `important`, `warning`, `caution`. Use them for the so-what sentence under a chart, or to flag a data problem you found.

## 6. Folded code

Every chunk on this site is folded by default (click "Code" to open it). That comes from one line in `_quarto.yml`: `code-fold: true`. Your published project should do the same: the story reads in front, the code is one click away for whoever wants to check it.

## What you now know

You can read any `.qmd` on this site. The Data and Exploration pages are just more of the same three ingredients, arranged into an analysis.
